title: A shabad for every moment
hookLine: Sikhs mark birth, marriage and death with particular hymns

cards: Hum the first song you danced to at a wedding. Now the one playing in the car the summer you were seventeen. Now the one they played at your grandfather's funeral.
Some songs get welded to moments like that: a private soundtrack. Sikh life has a shared one. The same hymns, sung at the same turning points, by family after family, generation after generation.
A child born, a couple married, a life ended: each has its hymns, and some children can hum them before they can read.

teach.h: SHABAD: A HYMN, AND THE WORD.
teach.b: The word is shabad. It means word, and in Sikh usage it means two things at once. A shabad is a hymn, one composition from the Guru Granth Sahib.
And the Shabad is the Word itself, the voice of the Guru, the presence of the One in sound. When a shabad is sung, Sikhs understand both are happening. These hymns are meant to be sung.

teach.h: ARRANGED BY RAAG, TO BE SUNG.
teach.b: The scripture is arranged by raag, musical mode, each with its own mood and, tradition says, its own time of day, and kirtan, singing the hymns with music, is at the heart of worship. Now look at a life.
When a child is born, there are shabads of joy and thanks. When a couple marries, they walk four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib while the lavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung.

At the end of every day, and at the end of a life, Kirtan Sohila is sung. Guru Nanak even wrote hymns for mourning, the alaahniaan, in Raag Vadhans on ang 578, which turn the old songs of lament toward the One.
For the next five weeks, this part of the path walks through shabads like these: about wealth and greed, longing and friendship, night and morning, birth, marriage and death.

teach.h: FIVE WEEKS OF SHABADS FOR A LIFE.
teach.b: Each is a hymn Sikhs reach for at a particular moment. The idea isn't to memorize a playlist.
It's to have, for every moment, words and a melody that point beyond the moment itself.

how: Sikhs sing shabads from the Guru Granth Sahib in kirtan, and mark life's turning points with particular hymns: shabads of thanks at a birth, the lavan at a wedding, Kirtan Sohila at night and at a funeral.

games.q: a couple is about to marry in the gurdwara. what happens at the center of the ceremony?
o: they walk four rounds while the lavan are sung.
games.why: four verses by Guru Ram Das, four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib. we'll walk them soon.

practice: Let one song tied to a memory play in your head, sacred or not, and notice where it takes you: a room, a face, a season. Kirtan works with that same pull of melody.
If you know any shabad, even its first line or a single Waheguru sung to a tune, let it play next; if not, rest in the silence after your song.

wordCard.voice: Shabad. A hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib, and the Word itself. Sikhs sing particular shabads at birth, marriage, the close of each day and the end of a life.
